Lake Merced dialect white-crowned sparrows

Lake Merced, San Francisco
song dialect
CommunicationMating

"In the Lake Merced region, between the years of 1969/1970 and 1990 the number of individuals singing the LM dialect decreased from 93 to 32 per cent while the individuals singing the SF dialect increased from 2 to 34 per cent." SF dialect has higher minimum frequency than LM, better adapted to...

Recorded from 1969 to 1990
Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Yes
Evidence and details

Description: "In the Lake Merced region, between the years of 1969/1970 and 1990 the number of individuals singing the LM dialect decreased from 93 to 32 per cent while the individuals singing the SF dialect increased from 2 to 34 per cent." SF dialect has higher minimum frequency than LM, better adapted to low-frequency urban noise (Luther & Baptista 2010)

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: suspected unknown

Oblique: From 1998 study in San Francisco, male sparrows learn songs of adult neighbors rather than fathers (Bell et al. 1998)

Domains: communication; mating

Anthropogenic effects: "Urban noise, which is louder at low frequencies, increased during our study period and therefore should have created a selection pressure for songs with higher frequencies. We found that the minimum frequency of songs increased both within and between dialects during the 30-year time span...We suggest that the observed change occurred as a result of more efficient transmission of songs with higher frequencies in an urban environment" (Luther & Baptista 2010)

Sources: [1] [2]

Vertical: UnknownHorizontal: UnknownOblique: Yes
Evidence and details

Description: "There was a large amount of turnover in the dialects sung by individuals in the Presidio and Lake Merced regions between 1969/1970 and the 1990s. In the Presidio, the P dialect went extinct, decreasing from 64 to 0 per cent between 1969/1970 and 1998, while the SF dialect increased from 29 to 95 per cent. The remaining birds sang P/SF hybrid songs" (Luther & Baptista 2010)

Vertical: suspected unknown

Horizontal: suspected unknown

Oblique: From 1998 study in San Francisco, male sparrows learn songs of adult neighbors rather than fathers (Bell et al. 1998)

Domains: communication; mating

Anthropogenic effects: "Urban noise, which is louder at low frequencies, increased during our study period and therefore should have created a selection pressure for songs with higher frequencies. We found that the minimum frequency of songs increased both within and between dialects during the 30-year time span...We suggest that the observed change occurred as a result of more efficient transmission of songs with higher frequencies in an urban environment" (Luther & Baptista 2010)
